newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper sees oil bonanza by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper sees oil bonanza by 2000.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper forecast Wednesday that Colombia's proven oil reserves would almost triple to 9 billion barrels by the year 2000 and said 80 percent of the country's potential oil-bearing regions were still unexplored.
Speaking in Yopal, in eastern Casanare province, center of British Petroleum's operations, Samper said Colombia
would continue to rely on private enterprise, participating alongside state-run Ecopetrol under clear and fair rules, if it was to take full advantage of the bonanza.

At the same event, Ecopetrol chairman Luis Bernardo Florez said BP's Cusiana and Cupiagua fields would be producing about 500,000 barrels a day, more than half Colombia's total daily output, by the end of 1998, up from current capacity of about 180,000 barrels a day.
"Between now and the year 2000 we will have accumulated (proven) reserves of about 9 billion barrels," Samper said.
"These reserves are concentrated in just a few wells because we have only explored 20 percent of the areas with promising oil potential," he added.

Samper acknowledged the challenge of putting into effect sensible, long-term oil management policies. In a report two weeks ago, the influential National Association of Financial Institutions (ANIF) criticized the government for not having any long-term strategy.

The president did not mention the government's on-going discussions with BP, Colombia's largest single foreign investor, which is looking for sweeter contract terms in a 287,000 hectare block of the Piedemonte region adjacent to Cusiana and Cupiagua.
But he recognized that Colombia was reliant on foreign multinationals if it was to fully exploit its oil wealth.

"The new dimensions of the oil industry in Colombia are beyond our financial and technological abilities, for which reason we need the active and permanent participation of private eneterpise in the entire chain of production," Samper said.

In the last six months, BP has been hit by a barrage of media allegations that it was linked to right-wing paramilitary groups, which have killed political dissidents in the province since the start of the decade.
BP has repeatedly denied the claims and Samper said Wednesday there was no evidence to support the accusations and praised the multinational for its contribution to regional development.
